name: HubSpot Service Hub
tagline: A help desk that lives inside a CRM rather than syncing with one — and prices its AI at $0.50 per resolved conversation instead of per ticket touched.
tldr: Service Hub is the customer-service layer of HubSpot's platform: a help desk workspace, ticketing, knowledge base, customer portal, surveys, and the Breeze Customer Agent, all sitting on the same Smart CRM record as marketing and sales data.

Pricing is per-seat and annual-first — Free (2 users), Starter at $7/seat/mo annually ($20 monthly), Professional at $90/seat/mo annually ($100 monthly), Enterprise at $150/seat/mo — plus mandatory one-time onboarding fees of $1,500 (Pro) and $3,500 (Enterprise).

The CRM tie-in is the real differentiator and it's concrete: a support agent opening a ticket sees the same contact record the sales rep and marketer see — lifecycle stage, deal history, email opens, form submissions — with no connector to configure, because there is no second system to connect to.

As of April 14, 2026 HubSpot moved Breeze Customer Agent to outcome-based pricing at 50 credits (about $0.50) per resolved conversation, down from $1.00 per conversation — a genuinely more buyer-friendly meter than Zendesk's or Intercom's undisclosed/higher per-resolution rates.

The weakness is depth: reviewers describe the ticketing UX and routing as thinner than dedicated help desks, and the native channel list (email, chat, forms, calling, WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger) has real gaps — no native Instagram DM or SMS in the help desk workspace.
Best for companies already running HubSpot CRM for sales or marketing, where the unified customer record is worth more than best-in-class ticketing depth.
keyFeatures: Help Desk workspace that turns incoming messages from every connected channel into tickets in a single queue
Breeze Customer Agent, an LLM-backed agent that resolves customer inquiries across email and live chat 24/7, billed per resolved conversation
Breeze Knowledge Base Agent that turns past support interactions into self-service knowledge base articles
Native ticketing on the HubSpot Smart CRM object model, so tickets associate directly to contacts, companies, and deals
Customer Success Workspace with health scores and account activity prioritisation for CSMs
Customizable NPS, CSAT, and custom feedback surveys tied back to the CRM record
SLA management with automated ticket routing to keep response and resolution times on target
Calling with IVR phone trees and team routing, plus Conversation Intelligence call analytics (Professional and above)
Customer Portal giving logged-in customers a secure view of their own ticket history

companyInfo.funding: Public — IPO'd on the NYSE (HUBS) in October 2014; revenue of US$2.63B in 2024

faq.question: What does HubSpot's Breeze Customer Agent actually cost?
faq.answer: Since April 14, 2026, HubSpot charges outcome-based: 50 HubSpot Credits per resolved conversation, which works out to roughly $0.50 at the $0.010-per-credit rate. HubSpot's own announcement frames this as a move 'from $1.00 per conversation to $0.50 per resolved conversation.' Conversations the system doesn't measure as resolved aren't charged. Included allowances are 500 credits on Starter, 3,000 on Professional, and 5,000 on Enterprise — so Professional's bundle covers roughly 60 resolutions a month before overages start.

faq.question: Do I need to already use HubSpot CRM to use Service Hub?
faq.answer: No, but it's the only scenario where it clearly wins. Service Hub is built on the same Smart CRM as Marketing and Sales Hub, so buying it standalone means paying for a platform whose main advantage — one shared customer record across the whole funnel — you're deliberately not using. If you want ticketing depth alone, dedicated help desks give you more of it per dollar.

faq.question: Which channels can I actually connect to the help desk?
faq.answer: HubSpot's own documentation lists chat, email, form, calling, custom, WhatsApp, and Facebook Messenger channels. Notably absent from that list: native Instagram DM and native SMS in the help desk workspace. WhatsApp and calling both require a Professional or Enterprise subscription.

faq.question: What are the hidden costs beyond the seat price?
faq.answer: Two that catch buyers out. First, Professional and Enterprise carry mandatory one-time onboarding fees of $1,500 and $3,500 respectively — real money on top of year-one seats. Second, HubSpot Credits reset monthly and don't roll over, so an unusually quiet month is credit you simply lose.

faq.question: Is the AI resolution rate HubSpot claims believable?
faq.answer: HubSpot's company-news post cites Customer Agent resolving 65% of conversations and cutting resolution time 39%. Treat that as a vendor figure from favourable deployments, not a baseline — it's the same category of claim as Zendesk's '80%+ automation', and independent reporting on this whole product class consistently finds fresh deployments landing far lower until the knowledge base is heavily curated. We found no independent audit of HubSpot's number.

faq.question: How does Service Hub compare to Zendesk on price?
faq.answer: Service Hub Professional at $90/seat/mo annually undercuts Zendesk Suite Professional at $115/agent/mo, and HubSpot publishes its per-resolution AI rate while Zendesk does not. But Zendesk's entry AI tier (Suite Team, $55/agent/mo) is cheaper than HubSpot's, and HubSpot's mandatory onboarding fee has no Zendesk equivalent.

criteriaScores.note: HubSpot's help desk documentation lists chat, email, form, calling, custom, WhatsApp, and Facebook Messenger as connectable channels — solid coverage of the core, but no native Instagram DM and no native SMS channel in the help desk workspace, both of which Zendesk covers (knowledge.hubspot.com/help-desk/connect-channels-to-help-desk).

Every connected channel creates a ticket in the same help desk workspace, and because tickets are CRM objects associated to a contact record, cross-channel history genuinely lands in one place rather than in per-channel inboxes. Marked down only because the channel set feeding that unified view is narrower than the leaders' (hubspot.com/products/service/help-desk).

Breeze Customer Agent is a genuine generative AI agent that resolves inquiries autonomously across email and live chat, not smart-reply suggestions — but it is gated to Professional and Enterprise subscriptions, so Starter and Free buyers get no autonomous AI at all (hubspot.com/products/service).

HubSpot's own company-news post claims Customer Agent 'resolves 65% of conversations and cuts resolution time by 39%'. We found no independent audit of that figure, and one reviewer (Bo L., VP of Customer Success, Computer Software) called the product 'behind the curve on AI' — enough divergence to withhold a high score.

SLA management with automated ticket routing is native, and Service Hub inherits HubSpot's full workflow engine — multi-step branching automations spanning tickets, contacts, deals, and marketing objects, not just per-ticket if/then triggers (hubspot.com/products/service).

The Help Desk workspace is a single pane across connected channels with the CRM record attached to every ticket, so agents see marketing and sales context inline. user feedback does flag interface clutter — one reviewer (Elizabeth B.) describes difficulty finding basic settings — so it is not the cleanest execution of the pattern.

Integration with HubSpot's own CRM is total because it IS the CRM — but that's the wrong question. For third-party CRMs, HubSpot ships a first-party Salesforce connector (bidirectional contact/account/opportunity sync) while Pipedrive and others are third-party marketplace builds, and HubSpot has an obvious structural incentive not to make rival CRMs first-class. A team standing on Salesforce should expect to run two customer records, not one.

Service Analytics provides real-time performance and satisfaction reporting, and customizable NPS, CSAT, and custom feedback surveys write back to the CRM record — meaning support metrics can be reported against revenue and lifecycle data in the same dashboard, which siloed help desks structurally cannot do (hubspot.com/products/service).

This is HubSpot's standout against its rivals: seat prices are published for every tier ($7/$90/$150 annually), the credit rate is published ($0.010/credit), and the AI resolution rate is published (50 credits ≈ $0.50 per resolved conversation) — where Zendesk publishes seats but not its resolution rate. Docked a point because credits reset monthly without rollover and the mandatory $1,500/$3,500 onboarding fees aren't visible in the headline seat price.

pricing.model: Per-seat tiered SaaS plus outcome-based AI billing via HubSpot Credits

plans.name: Free

plans.name: Starter
plans.notes: Includes 500 HubSpot Credits/mo; ticketing, knowledge base, customer portal, live chat, reporting dashboards — no Breeze Customer Agent

plans.name: Professional

plans.notes: Includes 5,000 HubSpot Credits/mo; adds skill-based routing, advanced analytics, higher platform limits. One-time $3,500 onboarding fee required

pricingBreakdown: HubSpot's pricing looks friendly and then quietly isn't, and it's worth separating the two halves. The AI half is the best-behaved meter in this category: 50 credits per resolved conversation at $0.010/credit is about $0.50, HubSpot publishes that number, and as of April 2026 you only pay when the conversation is actually measured as resolved. Compare that to Zendesk, which publishes seat prices but not its per-resolution rate at all — third-party trackers put it somewhere around $1.50-$2.00 — and HubSpot is doing something genuinely unusual by being legible. The seat half is where it gets murky. Professional at $90/seat/mo annually undercuts Zendesk Suite Professional at $115/agent/mo, but HubSpot then bolts on a mandatory one-time onboarding fee — $1,500 at Professional, $3,500 at Enterprise — that has no equivalent at Zendesk or Intercom. For a 10-seat team, year one at Professional is $10,800 in seats plus $1,500 onboarding, which is $12,300 before a single AI resolution overage. Two more traps: the $7 Starter price is annual-commitment-only and jumps to $20/seat month-to-month (a 186% swing), and credits reset monthly with no rollover, so quiet months are money you paid for and lost. The honest summary is that Service Hub's headline is cheaper than Zendesk's and its AI meter is fairer, but the true year-one number is closer than the sticker suggests.

capabilities.note: This is the whole argument for the product. Tickets are HubSpot CRM objects, so a ticket is associated to the contact, company, and deal records that sales and marketing already work in. A support agent sees lifecycle stage, open deals, and past marketing touches on the ticket without an integration existing anywhere in the picture — there is no second system, so there is nothing to sync, break, or reconcile at 2am. If your team currently maintains a Zendesk-to-CRM connector, this is the pain it removes.

The autonomous AI layer, resolving inquiries across email and live chat around the clock, gated to Professional and above. HubSpot claims 65% of conversations resolved; we found no independent verification of that figure, and at least one reviewer specifically calls the product 'behind the curve on AI'. Treat the vendor number as an aspiration for a well-curated knowledge base rather than a starting point.

A native knowledge base and a customer portal (secure, logged-in ticket history) feed both self-service and the AI agent. The Breeze Knowledge Base Agent closes the loop by drafting articles from resolved support interactions — a sensible answer to the perennial problem that knowledge bases rot because nobody has time to write them.

Chat, email, forms, calling, WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, and custom channels connect to the help desk. WhatsApp and calling both need Professional or higher. SLA-driven automated routing is native; skill-based routing is Enterprise-only. The gap versus dedicated help desks is real: no native Instagram DM and no native SMS channel in the help desk workspace.

Service Analytics covers real-time performance and satisfaction reporting, and NPS/CSAT/custom surveys write results back onto the CRM contact record. That last part is the quiet advantage — you can report CSAT against deal size, lifecycle stage, or acquisition channel in one dashboard, which a support tool sitting outside the CRM cannot do without a data warehouse in between.

pros: The CRM tie-in is structural, not an integration — tickets are CRM objects, so support agents see sales and marketing history on the record with nothing to configure and nothing to break

The most transparent AI pricing in this category: published seat prices, a published credit rate, and a published $0.50-per-resolved-conversation figure, where Zendesk publishes no resolution rate at all
Outcome-based AI billing since April 2026 means unresolved conversations aren't chargeable — a genuinely better deal structure than paying per conversation touched
Support metrics (NPS, CSAT, custom surveys) land on the same contact record as revenue data, enabling CX reporting against pipeline that siloed help desks can't do natively
Free tier for two users and a $7/seat Starter make it unusually cheap to actually try before committing
cons: Ticketing depth and UX draw specific criticism — one reviewer (VP of Customer Success) calls it 'Poor UX for support ticketing, lacking in core functionality, behind the curve on AI'
Mandatory one-time onboarding fees of $1,500 (Professional) and $3,500 (Enterprise) are real, unavoidable year-one costs with no Zendesk or Intercom equivalent
Native channel coverage has gaps a dedicated help desk wouldn't — no Instagram DM, no SMS in the help desk workspace — and WhatsApp and calling are locked behind Professional
Credits reset monthly with no rollover, so under-usage is money burned rather than banked
If you're standing on Salesforce or Pipedrive rather than HubSpot CRM, the product's central advantage evaporates and you're back to maintaining two customer records

bestFor: Companies already running HubSpot CRM for sales or marketing who want support on the same customer record
Mid-market teams that want a published, predictable per-resolution AI price rather than a negotiated one
Customer success orgs that need health scores and CSAT reporting tied to revenue data, not just ticket metrics
Small teams testing the water — the free two-user tier and $7 Starter make evaluation genuinely low-risk
verdict: Service Hub is one of the few tools on this list where the pitch and the reality actually line up, provided you're the right buyer. The CRM argument isn't marketing spin: tickets are CRM objects, so a support agent opening a ticket sees the deal, the lifecycle stage, and the marketing history without an integration existing at all. If you've ever debugged a Zendesk-to-CRM sync at 2am, you know exactly what that's worth. And HubSpot is doing something in AI pricing that its rivals aren't — publishing the number. $0.50 per resolved conversation, only charged when the conversation actually resolves, against Zendesk's rate that you can't find anywhere on their site. That's a real difference in how a vendor treats you. But the criticism is specific and it's from the right kind of reviewer: a VP of Customer Success calling it 'poor UX for support ticketing, lacking in core functionality, behind the curve on AI.' That's not a grumble about onboarding — that's someone saying the core job is thinner than a dedicated help desk. The channel list backs it up: no Instagram DM, no SMS in the workspace. And I can't verify HubSpot's 65% resolution claim; there's no independent audit of it that I could find, so treat it as a ceiling, not a baseline. Buy this if you're already on HubSpot CRM. If you're on Salesforce, the entire argument collapses and you should be comparing Zendesk instead.
